items.prompt: What is documentation discipline?
choices: Recording every conversation held at work
A private list of colleagues' errors
Confirming verbal decisions in writing
items.explanation: It is the habit of confirming decisions in writing, not surveillance or blame-collecting.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, what exactly was the engineer's problem?
choices: The decision lived only in two memories
They had disobeyed the director's instruction
They shipped before schedule
items.explanation: The engineer followed the instruction. What was missing was any record of it.

items.prompt: Besides lying, what can make the director's account differ?
choices: A change in company policy since last month
A sincere memory gap about a hallway chat
A different job title for the engineer
items.explanation: People honestly forget conversations they did not think mattered at the time.

items.prompt: An undocumented dispute is usually settled by what?
choices: A coin toss between the two accounts
The account that was given first
Whoever is more senior in the room
items.explanation: With no evidence, the room defaults to rank, not to what actually happened.

items.prompt: Does following an instruction protect you on its own?
choices: No, because you cannot show it was instructed
Yes, since following orders is always a defense
Yes, as long as the feature passed testing
items.explanation: Compliance protects you only if the instruction can be shown.

items.prompt: What is a paper trail?
choices: One email sent after an incident has begun
Written records of what was decided
A log of late arrivals
items.explanation: It is the accumulated set of confirmations and notes that establish decisions.

items.prompt: What is 'CYA done well' mainly about?
choices: Collecting proof so you can blame a colleague
Avoiding any risky decision
A shared, accurate record for everyone
items.explanation: Its purpose is a shared, accurate record, which also protects the person who gave the instruction.

items.prompt: When is a verbal decision best written down?
choices: Soon after it happens, while fresh
Only once a dispute has already started
At quarter end, in a review
items.explanation: Fresh, prompt records read as routine and are the most accurate.

items.prompt: Two engineers each hear a director say 'hold the release a week'. One sends a same-day note; the other relies on memory. Three weeks later the director says 'I said two weeks.' Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Both are equally protected, because the director's statement can't be checked either way
The first has a dated document; the second has only competing memories
Neither is protected; a note only shows what the sender believed
The second is better off, since nothing written can be used against them
items.explanation: The note moves the first engineer's case from memory to a dated document. The second has only an account that rank can override. A note is not a guarantee, but it changes what the dispute is about.
items.reference:
Same decision, two outcomes
🗣️ Spoken only: two memories, no way to check
📄 Written same day: one dated record
⚖️ Without a record, rank settles the dispute
Why: a verbal decision lives only in memory, and an honest memory gap is as damaging as a lie.
items.learnMore:
A verbal decision lives only in memory

Right after a hallway decision both people agree on it. Weeks later each remembers a version, and the disagreement is settled by credibility, which usually follows rank. Documentation discipline moves the decision from memory into a dated record, so it does not depend on who argues more confidently. It also protects against sincere forgetting, not only bad faith.

Common mistake

Assuming that because you followed an instruction, the instruction can be shown.
items.reflection: Think of a decision you once acted on that was never written down. Who else remembers it, and would they tell it the same way?

items.prompt: Which claim about why documentation matters is best supported by the Scenario?
choices: It exists mainly to catch people who are knowingly lying to avoid blame
It matters only when the other person is already hostile to you
It replaces following instructions carefully
It guards against sincere memory gaps as well as bad faith
items.explanation: The director need not be lying: hallway talk is easy to misremember. Treating the habit as protection against ordinary forgetting is also what keeps it from feeling accusatory.

items.prompt: A director sincerely forgot the hallway instruction. What does a same-day note from the engineer do for the director?
choices: Proves they acted in bad faith when they denied it
Gives them a neutral reminder without accusing them
Forces them to defend the decision publicly right away
Moves the responsibility for the decision to the engineer
items.explanation: A neutral dated note works as a reminder to an honest person and as a record for everyone else. It protects the director from an accidental false statement too.

items.prompt: Which framing reads as professional?
choices: Just confirming what we agreed, for my notes
Putting this on record in case you deny it
So there is proof when it goes wrong, as I warned
items.explanation: Neutral note-taking language reads as routine; anticipating a denial reads as paranoid.

items.prompt: Who should be the primary recipient of a confirmation?
choices: That person's manager, so it carries weight
The person who gave the instruction
A wide group including several other teams
items.explanation: Direct and primary to the decision-maker keeps it a record, not a campaign.

items.prompt: When does a confirmation read as routine practice?
choices: When it is sent once a problem has surfaced
When it is sent just before a review meeting
When it is sent soon after the conversation
items.explanation: Timing close to the conversation is what makes it look like habit.

items.prompt: Which tone fits a good confirmation?
choices: Short and neutral, restating the facts
Detailed and defensive, anticipating an argument
Formal and legalistic, citing every policy
items.explanation: Short and neutral avoids editorializing.

items.prompt: What mostly decides paranoid versus professional?
choices: Whether anything was written down at all
Framing, audience and timing
How long the sender has been employed
items.explanation: The act of writing is the same either way; the delivery differs.

items.prompt: Cc'ing people who were not in the conversation tends to do what?
choices: Show how open and transparent you are
Make the message easier to find later
Signal that you are building a case
items.explanation: A wider audience implies the record is for someone other than the decision-maker.

items.prompt: A confirmation sent only after trouble surfaced reads as what?
choices: Reactive and defensive
Thorough and routine
Neutral and easily forgotten
items.explanation: After the incident, any note looks like a reaction to it.

items.prompt: Which opening is more professional?
choices: For the record, since you tend to forget:
Confirming what we just discussed:
As I already warned you, in writing:
items.explanation: Neutral restatement beats pointed or accusing openings.

items.prompt: Four drafts record the same decision. Which is least likely to read as paranoid?
choices: Sent to the director alone that afternoon: 'Confirming we will ship without the review and schedule it after launch.'
Sent to the director and their manager that afternoon: 'Confirming for the record that you instructed us to skip the review.'
Sent to the director alone a week after the incident: 'Confirming we shipped without the review, as you instructed.'
Sent to the whole team that afternoon: 'To avoid confusion later, the director has decided to skip the review.'
items.explanation: It goes only to the decision-maker, soon after, in a neutral tone. The others add an audience, a delay, or an accusing frame.
items.reference:
Same facts, different framing
✅ To the instruction-giver, right after, short and neutral
⚠️ Cc'd to managers, sent after trouble, defensive in tone
🧭 Framing, audience, timing, tone decide the reading
Why: the act of writing is neutral; it reads as paranoid because of how, to whom and when it is sent.
items.learnMore:
Framing, audience, timing and tone

A confirmation reads as professional when it goes directly to the person who gave the instruction, soon after the conversation, in a short neutral tone that restates facts. It reads as paranoid when it is sent to a wider audience, only after trouble has started, or phrased as if anticipating a denial. The closer to the conversation it is sent, the more it looks like routine practice.

Common mistake

Believing the problem is writing it down at all, rather than how it is sent.
items.reflection: Recall a message you received that felt like someone was building a case. Which of framing, audience, timing or tone made it feel that way?

items.prompt: The demo's teaching model gives 100 minus 5 points per day of delay, with a floor of 10. What does it say about a confirmation sent after 6 days, and after 20 days?
choices: About 30% routine at 6 days; the 10% floor at 20 days
About 70% routine at 6 days; 0% at 20 days
About 70% routine at 6 days; the 10% floor at 20 days
About 94% routine at 6 days; 80% at 20 days
items.explanation: 6 days: 100 - 30 = 70. 20 days: 100 - 100 = 0, which the floor lifts to 10. This is a teaching model, not measured data.

items.prompt: You send a routine same-day note to the director, who replies, 'Why are you putting this in writing?' Which response best keeps the tone professional?
choices: Say it is how you track your commitments, and invite corrections
Explain that earlier disputes have taught you not to trust verbal agreements
Apologize and promise to stop confirming decisions in writing
Forward the exchange to their manager so the reply is visible
items.explanation: Framing it as your own notes and inviting correction keeps it a shared record. Citing distrust, backing off entirely, or widening the audience each undermine it.

items.prompt: When does a decision most call for a written confirmation?
choices: When the speaker has a senior title
When the conversation ran for a long time
When stakes and ambiguity are both high
items.explanation: Both stakes and ambiguity matter together, not length or title.

items.prompt: A teammate agrees to rename a variable that the diff will show. Is a confirmation needed?
choices: No, stakes are tiny and the diff is the record
Yes, every verbal decision needs one in writing
Yes, because it is a code change
items.explanation: Low stakes and no ambiguity mean little need.

items.prompt: Documenting literally everything tends to do what?
choices: Protect you more completely in every dispute
Bury the decisions that actually matter
Make colleagues trust you more
items.explanation: Over-documenting reads as excessive and dilutes the important records.

items.prompt: Low stakes but high ambiguity. What is the documentation need?
choices: High, since the details are unclear
Maximum, because ambiguity alone decides it
Low, since little rides on it
items.explanation: Both factors must be high for the need to climb.

items.prompt: High stakes, but the decision is already recorded and unambiguous. What is the need?
choices: Low, since a record already exists
High, since the stakes are very high
Maximum, since it matters a lot
items.explanation: Stakes alone are not enough if there is nothing to misremember.

items.prompt: Why did the Scenario's decision call for a trail?
choices: The director seemed to be in a bad mood
High stakes and an easy-to-misremember hallway chat
It was said out loud rather than typed, which counts less
items.explanation: Skipping a security review is high stakes, and a passing remark is easy to forget.

items.prompt: Which has the lowest documentation need?
choices: A verbal approval to skip a security review
A verbal promise of a deadline extension
A trivial rename shown in the code diff
items.explanation: The rename is low stakes and already recorded.

items.prompt: In the demo, need = stakes x ambiguity / 100. If one of them is zero, the need is what?
choices: Zero
Equal to the other value
items.explanation: Anything multiplied by zero is zero.

items.prompt: Using the demo's model (stakes x ambiguity / 100), which pair gives the highest documentation need?
choices: Stakes 70, ambiguity 80
Stakes 90, ambiguity 50
Stakes 100, ambiguity 40
Stakes 30, ambiguity 100
items.explanation: 70x80/100 = 56; 90x50/100 = 45; 100x40/100 = 40; 30x100/100 = 30. Balanced high values beat one extreme.
items.reference:
When a trail is worth it
🔥 High stakes + hard to remember: send a confirmation
🧊 Low stakes or already recorded: skip it
🧮 Demo score = stakes x ambiguity / 100
Why: documenting everything buries the decisions that matter, so aim at stakes and ambiguity together.
items.learnMore:
Stakes and ambiguity together

A written confirmation earns its cost when two things hold: a lot rides on the decision if it is misremembered, and it would be hard to recall exactly without help. If either is low, such as a trivial change that the code diff already records, a confirmation adds noise. In the demo's model the need score is stakes times ambiguity divided by 100, so it stays low unless both are high.

Common mistake

Treating every verbal agreement as needing a record, which makes you look like you log everything.
items.reflection: List two decisions you made verbally this week. Where does each fall on stakes and on how easily it could be misremembered?

items.prompt: Which verbal decision most clearly calls for a short written confirmation?
choices: A teammate agreeing to rename a function the pull request already shows
Two colleagues agreeing where to eat lunch on Friday
A manager saying in passing you may skip a compliance step
Moving a meeting by 30 minutes on a shared calendar
items.explanation: Only the compliance exception combines high stakes with a remark that is easy to misremember. The others are low stakes or already recorded.

High, since every approval should also be emailed
High, since tickets cannot be trusted as records
None, since a senior person's word is enough
items.explanation: The ticket already holds the decision, the author and the date, so there is little left to misremember. The need depends on what record exists, not on rank.

items.prompt: What must a strong confirmation restate?
choices: That a conversation took place
The specific decision that was made
How you felt about how the meeting went
items.explanation: The decision itself must be in writing.

items.prompt: Which message is weak?
choices: Confirming: the review is deferred until after launch.
Confirming we will ship without the review this sprint.
Thanks for the chat earlier!
items.explanation: It records that a chat happened, not what was agreed.

items.prompt: Where does the date of the record come from?
choices: The message's own timestamp
A footer you must type by hand
It is not part of a record
items.explanation: Sending it promptly means the timestamp supplies the date.

items.prompt: A reply of 'Got it, thanks!' is what kind of evidence?
choices: A full restatement of the decision
Partial: receipt without objection
Proof the decision was wise
items.explanation: It shows they saw your message, nothing more.

items.prompt: Should the message say 'in case this comes up later'?
choices: Yes, so the reader understands why you wrote
Yes, in bold type
No, the record speaks for itself
items.explanation: That phrasing turns a routine note into a defensive one.

items.prompt: Should a confirmation include the reasoning given for the decision?
choices: Yes, if a reason was given
Always invent one to be safe
Never, reasons only cause arguments
items.explanation: Include the stated reason when there is one; do not invent.

items.prompt: 'Following up on our conversation about the timeline' is weak because?
choices: It is too short to be read
It does not state what was decided
It is addressed to only one person
items.explanation: Nothing in it could be checked later.

items.prompt: What does ending with 'Let me know if I've got that wrong' do?
choices: Threatens the reader with consequences
Cancels the value of the record entirely if used
Invites correction without accusing anyone
items.explanation: It frames the note as checking understanding.

items.prompt: Which confirmation of a verbal decision to cut the audit-log feature from this release is strongest?
choices: Thanks for the quick chat about scope!
Following up on scope for this release. Let me know what you think when you can, no rush at all.
As discussed, things are moving along nicely on the release, and I will keep you posted as it goes.
Confirming: audit-log work is cut from this release and moves to the next, per your call given the schedule.
items.explanation: Only the first states the decision and the reason. The others record that a talk happened.
items.reference:
Weak versus strong
🚫 'Thanks for the chat earlier!': records only that a talk happened
✅ 'Confirming: review deferred until after launch': records the decision
📅 The message's timestamp supplies the date
Why: the specific decision must be in writing; a note that something happened records nothing.
items.learnMore:
What a confirmation must contain

A strong confirmation names the specific decision and, if one was given, the reason. The timestamp supplies the date, and the message does not need to say it is for later use. A reply like 'Got it, thanks!' shows receipt without objection, but only gains meaning from being attached to your detailed message, so the discipline starts with whoever writes the detailed version.

Common mistake

Sending a friendly note that never states what was decided.
items.reflection: Rewrite a recent 'thanks for the chat' style message so that it states the decision. What did you have to commit to saying?

items.prompt: You send a detailed confirmation and receive only 'Got it, thanks!' Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Their reply alone proves they approved the decision as stated
Together they show you stated it and they did not object
Their reply makes your message redundant
Silence would have been stronger evidence than their reply was
items.explanation: The reply carries meaning only because it sits under your message, which restates the decision.

items.prompt: In Version A, whose account wins by default?
choices: The engineer's, who acted
Neither; the review stalls
The more senior person's
items.explanation: Without evidence, rank-based credibility decides.

items.prompt: In Version B, what does the room have to go on?
choices: A dated written record from day 0
Two memories that are 21 days old
A transcript of the hallway talk
items.explanation: The confirmation was sent at the time.

items.prompt: Does Version B remove the director's incentive to deny it?
choices: Yes, completely, since the record is dated
No, it only settles the factual question
Yes, but only if it is sent in writing
items.explanation: Incentives remain; the record changes what can be argued.

items.prompt: Does Version B's email blame anyone?
choices: Yes, quietly, in how it is phrased
Yes, by naming the director as responsible
No, it neutrally restates the decision
items.explanation: Its tone is routine note-taking.

items.prompt: An undocumented dispute usually gets settled by what?
choices: Power rather than fact
Fact, once people calm down
A quick vote
items.explanation: It is resolved, but by rank, often unnoticed.

items.prompt: In Version A, where does the engineer end up?
choices: Fully cleared of responsibility
Carrying a decision someone else made
Promoted for following orders
items.explanation: They cannot correct the record afterwards.

items.prompt: In the demo's model, a confirmation at 21 days of delay reads as routine at what level?
items.explanation: 100 - 5x21 is below 10, so the floor of 10 applies.

items.prompt: Where does the confirmation's protective power come from?
choices: Being dated and sent at the time
Winning an argument in the review
Being cc'd to senior leaders
items.explanation: It never has to argue; it only has to exist.

items.prompt: In Version B, the director says at the review, 'I don't remember saying that.' What does the written record do?
choices: Proves the director lied on purpose
Settles what was said, whatever the director remembers
Has no effect, since the director is more senior than the engineer
Matters only if the engineer argues loudly too
items.explanation: The record answers the factual question independent of anyone's memory or rank. It says nothing about intent.
items.reference:
Version A versus Version B at day 21
🅰️ No trail: two memories, rank decides
🅱️ Day-0 confirmation: a dated document answers 'what was said'
🔁 Disagreement about the decision's wisdom remains
Why: a contemporaneous record answers the factual question, not the question of whether the decision was good.
items.learnMore:
What a record changes in the room

Without a record, the review has two accounts and defaults to the more credible one, usually the more senior. With a dated confirmation, the question 'what was said' is answered by a document. Incentives to avoid blame remain, so the director may still say they do not recall it, but the room is no longer choosing between memories. The email protects by existing, not by arguing.

Common mistake

Expecting the record to stop the other person from disagreeing with you.
items.reflection: Think of a past dispute at work. Which facts were settled by a document, and which were left to competing memories?

items.prompt: Which phrasing suits a much more senior person?
choices: Just want to make sure I understood correctly
Please confirm you are accountable for this call
Noting this for my records against you
items.explanation: Checking your own understanding avoids holding them accountable.

items.prompt: Is skipping documentation of senior decisions a sound instinct?
choices: Yes, avoid questioning more senior people
No, those are often higher stakes
Yes, etiquette requires it
items.explanation: More authority behind a decision often means more at stake.

items.prompt: Cc'ing people who were not in the conversation does what?
choices: Reads as polite
Is required for the record
Reads as building a case
items.explanation: It signals an audience beyond the decision-maker.

items.prompt: Does a written confirmation stop the other person from pushing back?
choices: No, it only fixes what was said
Yes, it ends the debate for good
Yes, once it is sent
items.explanation: Disagreement shifts to the substance of the decision.

items.prompt: Does this unit give legal advice?
choices: Yes, it covers any workplace dispute you face
No; ask HR or a lawyer for legal questions
Yes, but only for contracts
items.explanation: It covers workplace habits, not law.

items.prompt: If an instruction contradicts a compliance policy, what happens to the stakes?
choices: They fall, since policy decides
They stay the same; nothing else is needed
They rise sharply, so framing matters more
items.explanation: A note that sounds accusatory there risks being taken as a threat.

items.prompt: Why does a larger power gap raise the framing risk?
choices: Upward notes are rarer and can seem presumptuous
Senior people rarely read email carefully, so notes are missed
Senior people prefer much longer messages
items.explanation: The habit is the same, but tone needs more care.

items.prompt: A VP tells you in a corridor to delay a data-retention fix. Which approach best applies the unit?
choices: Cc the VP's manager so the note carries weight
Send the VP a short, direct note checking you understood, no cc
Skip it, since questioning a VP risks seeming presumptuous
Send a long note listing every risk and who is to blame if it fails
items.explanation: Direct, short and framed as checking understanding keeps it professional. Cc'ing escalates, skipping leaves no trail, and a long note reads as a case.
items.reference:
Adapting the habit upward
🎯 Direct to the senior person, no cc to their manager
✏️ Short, framed as checking your own understanding
⚖️ Not legal advice; HR or a lawyer for compliance conflicts
Why: a bigger power gap makes tone matter more, not documentation matter less.
items.learnMore:
Documenting upward, and the limits

The mechanics stay the same with a much more senior decision-maker, but the framing risk rises because people send these upward less often. Address the person directly, keep it short, and phrase it as checking your own understanding. Avoiding the note because the person is senior is backward, as those decisions are often higher stakes. A confirmation does not stop pushback, and it is not legal advice; for compliance conflicts, consult HR or a lawyer.

Common mistake

Skipping documentation precisely when the decision-maker is most senior.
items.reflection: Who is the most senior person you have taken an instruction from verbally? How would you have worded a note to them?

items.prompt: Which wording best fits a confirmation to a very senior person?
choices: Please acknowledge in writing, for our records, that you personally directed us to defer the retention fix.
Noting for the file that this was your call and that I only followed it.
Documenting your instruction now in case this is questioned later on.
Confirming I understood: we will defer the retention fix to next quarter. Tell me if I've got it wrong.
items.explanation: It restates the decision neutrally and invites correction. The others shift blame or anticipate a dispute.

items.prompt: After your confirmation, the director replies, 'That is not what I meant, we still do the review.' How should you read this?
choices: The record failed because the director now disagrees with you in writing
The record worked: the disagreement surfaced on day 0, not day 21
You should withdraw the note so it does not cause conflict
You should now cc their manager to settle it
items.explanation: Surfacing a misunderstanding early is the best outcome. The disagreement was there anyway; the note exposed it while it was cheap to fix.
